newsitem.title: UK: Labour plans would tear Britain apart - Major.
newsitem.headline: Labour plans would tear Britain apart - Major.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major, making probably his last big speech to parliament before an election, accused his Labour opponents on Thursday of adopting a blueprint for constitutional change that would tear Britain apart.

Reviving a theme which he believes swung the 1992 election his way, Major lashed Labour's commitment to give Scotland and Wales their own parliaments, saying the policy was fatally flawed and had been proposed for narrow party political reasons.
"Labour have given in to the temptation to put party before country," he said in a debate on Britain's constitutional future.
"The plans drawn up by the Labour Party...are a blueprint that would undermine the unity of the United Kingdom and erode the authority of parliament."

Major said Britain's constitution was the foundation of its democracy, freedoms and prosperity. "That is why I would defend it and would only change it cautiously and after careful examination. It should not be a plaything for party gain."

Major is convinced his decision to attack Labour on constitutional reform during the 1992 election campaign helped him to woo over vital voters and win a 21-seat parliamentary majority for his Conservative party.

The Conservatives chose to stage Thursday's debate, and, most unusually, to field Major as their principal speaker in it, in the hope that he could work similar magic ahead of the 1997 election, expected on May 1.

But Labour leader Tony Blair said Major could no longer scare Britons back into the Conservative fold by claiming that separate parliaments for Scotland and Wales would lead inevitably to their independence.
"The Conservatives no longer frighten because they are no longer believed," he said.
Labour, now 18 points ahead in opinion polls, is committed to a wide range of constitutional change in addition to setting up Scottish and Welsh parliaments.

It proposes to end the right of hereditary peers to sit in the upper House of London, introduce a Bill of Rights and a Freedom of Information Act and hold a referendum on whether to change Britain's first-past-the-post election system.
Blair questioned Major's reasons for holding the debate. "The Conservatives say it is to preserve the British constitution. I say it is more to preserve the Tory (Conservative) party," he said.

Britain was the only Western country where some people sat in parliament by virtue of birth rather than election, he said, adding: "The Tory party has always been the party which wants to horde power in the hands of a small elite."
